Module 1.title: Sustainability Concepts, SDGs and Clean Development Mechanism
Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Sustainability & SDGs
  • Brundtland Definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
  • Three Pillars of Sustainability: Social (equity, human health), Environmental (biodiversity, emissions), Economic (resource efficiency, circularity).
  • UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 17 Goals adopted in 2015 for 2030 Agenda (SDG 7: Affordable Clean Energy, SDG 9: Industry & Innovation, SDG 12: Responsible Consumption, SDG 13: Climate Action).
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Module 1 Reference: Sustainable Concepts

Clean Development Mechanism (CDM): Emission-reduction projects in developing nations earning certified emission reduction (CER) credits under the Kyoto Protocol.
Module 1.textbook_html:
1.1 The Triple Bottom Line of Sustainable Engineering

Sustainable engineering integrates environmental stewardship, economic viability, and social responsibility into engineering design processes. The Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework demands that engineered systems be evaluated not merely on financial profit, but on planetary and social impacts.

Module 2.title: Renewable and Non-Conventional Energy Systems
Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Renewable Energy Technologies
  • Solar Thermal vs Photovoltaic: Solar PV directly converts photons to DC electricity via semiconductor p-n junctions ($E > E_g$). Solar thermal concentrates radiation to generate steam for Rankine turbines.
  • Wind Energy: Power extracted $P = \frac{1}{2} \rho A V^3 C_p$. Betz Limit: Maximum theoretical aerodynamic efficiency $C_{p,max} = 16/27 \approx 59.3\%$.
  • Fuel Cells: Electrochemical conversion of chemical fuel directly to electricity without combustion ($2H_2 + O_2 \to 2H_2O + \text{Electricity} + \text{Heat}$). High thermodynamic efficiency ($\eta > 60\%$).
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Module 2 Reference: Renewable Energy

Biofuels: First generation (food crops), Second generation (non-food lignocellulosic biomass), Third generation (algae lipid extraction with high yield).
Module 2.textbook_html:
2.1 Renewable Energy Resources and Betz Wind Power Limit

Transitioning away from fossil fuels requires high-efficiency non-conventional energy harvesting. The power potential of wind is cubic with velocity ($P \propto V^3$), bounded by the theoretical Betz limit derived from momentum conservation across an actuator disk.

Module 3.title: Environmental Management, ISO 14001 and Life Cycle Analysis (LCA)
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: ISO 14001 & LCA
  • ISO 14001:2015: International standard for Environmental Management Systems (EMS) based on the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) continuous improvement cycle.
  • Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) Framework (ISO 14040):
    1. Goal and Scope Definition (Functional unit, system boundary: Cradle-to-Grave vs Cradle-to-Cradle).
    2. Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) Analysis (quantifying all raw material inputs and emission outputs).
    3. Life Cycle Impact Assessment (LCIA) (translating emissions into Global Warming Potential, Acidification).
    4. Interpretation (decision support for design improvement).
  • Carbon Footprint: Total greenhouse gas emissions expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent ($CO_2e$).
Module 3.detailed_notes:
Module 3 Reference: LCA

Circular Economy principles replace linear take-make-dispose paradigm with closed-loop industrial ecology: design for disassembly, remanufacturing, and biological nutrient recovery.
Module 3.textbook_html:
3.1 ISO 14040 Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) Methodology

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is an internationally standardized analytical methodology used to evaluate the comprehensive environmental burdens associated with a product, process, or service across its entire lifespan—from raw material extraction ("cradle") through processing, distribution, use, to final disposal or recycling ("grave").

Module 4.title: Pollution Control, Solid Waste Management and Hazardous Materials
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Pollution Control
  • Air Pollution Control: Electrostatic Precipitators (ESP, particulate removal $>99\%$), Cyclone separators (centrifugal removal of coarse dust), Flue Gas Desulfurization (FGD scrubbers for $SO_x$).
  • Water Quality Parameters: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD). Typical $COD > BOD$. Primary, secondary (activated sludge biological), and tertiary treatment.
  • Solid Waste Hierarchy: Reduce $\to$ Reuse $\to$ Recycle $\to$ Recover Energy $\to$ Landfill.
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Module 4 Reference: Waste Management

Electronic Waste (E-waste) handling, heavy metal recovery (gold, copper, rare earths), toxic leachate prevention in sanitary engineered landfills.
Module 4.textbook_html:
4.1 Industrial Emission Abatement and Wastewater Treatment

Industrial manufacturing generates gaseous, aqueous, and particulate effluents requiring rigorous engineering intervention to comply with national and state pollution control board regulations.

Module 5.title: Sustainable Habitat, Green Buildings and Environmental Regulations
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Green Buildings & Habitat
  • Green Building Rating Systems: LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design), GRIHA (Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment, India), IGBC.
  • Key Assessment Parameters: Sustainable site planning, Water efficiency (rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse), Energy performance (HVAC optimization, passive solar architecture, high-efficiency envelope), Materials selection (low VOC paints, recycled aggregates).
  • Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): Mandatory formal statutory process predicting environmental consequences of proposed infrastructure projects prior to granting clearance.
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Module 5 Reference: Green Habitats

Passive solar building design: Daylighting orientation, thermal mass walls, shading overhangs reducing artificial air conditioning loads.
Module 5.textbook_html:
5.1 Green Building Architecture & Sustainable Habitat Design

The built environment consumes more than $40\%$ of global electricity and produces one-third of total greenhouse gas emissions. Green building design integrates passive bioclimatic architecture, high-efficiency envelope engineering, and sustainable materials to reduce life-cycle environmental impact.
